title: Ultracompact double white dwarf binaries (e.g. eRASSU J060839.5-704014): what the astrophysics literature and mission documentation support as research sites and safe standoff distances
question: What do the peer-reviewed astrophysics literature and official mission documentation establish about ultracompact double-degenerate / AM CVn binaries — orbital-decay (Pdot) and gravitational-wave emission, tidal and direct-impact accretion physics, X-ray and timing observability, and detectability as LISA verification binaries — and what standoff distances, measurement requirements and instrument classes follow for gravitational-wave, X-ray/timing and chirp-measurement research posts, so that NOXIA can use a system such as eRASSU J060839.5-704014 (P = 374.15013(2) s, Pdot = -4.7(1) x 10^-11 s/s) as a scientifically plausible research site and mission target without inventing physics or guessing safe measurement distances?
why_now: This is an open worldbuilding_science request (external-tasks/open/EXT-KG-NOXIA-20260924-ultracompact-white-dwarf-research-sites.md) that names a specific real object and explicitly asks for a science/worldbuilding contract and 'sensible safety/measurement distances' before any gameplay mechanic is fixed. Its declared KG source of truth, docs/KG-0025-ULTRACOMPACT-WHITE-DWARF-BINARIES.md, is not present in this repository, so the object parameters (P, Pdot, direct-impact interpretation) are asserted in-repo but not backstopped here.
real_world_anchor: Ultracompact double white dwarf / AM CVn binaries and direct-impact accretors, concretely eRASSU J060839.5-704014 (P = 374.15013(2) s, Pdot = -4.7(1) x 10^-11 s/s); gravitational-wave emission and LISA verification-binary observability; X-ray/timing observations (NICER, Einstein Probe) and orbital-decay/chirp measurement campaigns.
novelty_reason: Not covered by any previous topic: prior astronomy work addressed real solar-system bodies and Hohmann travel (RES-20260828-BF7F1B4D) and launch-site/orbital-access criteria (RES-20260913-1E741E90). This gap concerns Galactic compact-binary astrophysics (accretion physics, gravitational-wave emission, LISA verification binaries, observability and safe standoff distances), which the earlier candidates do not touch.
